Hi Kimberly,

Thanks for taking this. We're finalizing the requirements for moving our inference workloads into a private deployment with Redwood. The main ask from our side is: provide a recommendation for network connectivity given the attached topology. Specifically we need pros/cons and operational implications for three patterns: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site (IPSec) VPN.

Key constraints:
- We need source-IP visibility for downstream app logs and for some internal rate-limiting hooks.
- Compliance requires minimal cross-account exposure; audit logs must show client IPs where possible.
- Our security team prefers predictable control over ingress and egress rules.
- Expected baseline TPS is ~120 req/s with occasional bursts to 350 req/s for a 10–15 min window.

Can you outline a recommended path and an operational checklist (DNS, certs, MTU/NAT, monitoring) and any lead-time or procurement items we should plan for?

Thanks,
Sara
Sara Hart
Head of Cloud & Architecture, Aegis Retail

Hi Sara — thanks for the clear brief and the topology. I pulled together a short summary and a suggested next step (30-min design call) — see attachment for the one-page pros/cons and a rough ops checklist. High level here:

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- PrivateLink (interface endpoint) is the safest from a blast-radius and permissions perspective for cross-account private deploys; gives you explicit ENI-based access and works well with our Private control plane.
- Site-to-site VPN is a straightforward fallback for bursty/backup traffic or for customers who require an IPsec tunnel terminated into our edge gateway; it adds management and longer lead times for HA.
- VPC peering can give true L3 reachability and preserve source IPs without NAT, but it requires cross-account peering setup and careful routing controls — it increases surface area and is harder to scale multi-region.

I recommended we run PrivateLink as primary, with an optional VPN fallback for burst overflow and day-1 access for your infra team. Attachment includes checklist items: DNS (private hosted zones), certs (mutual TLS at the app level), NACL/SG rules, expected egress charges, and monitoring hooks for token-level latency/cost.

Can we schedule a short working session tomorrow to walk the ops checklist with your network team? I can include Ben Carter (networking lead) and Marcus Lin (deploy ops) from our side.

Best,
Kimberly Park
Solutions Architect — Redwood Inference

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-11-13T13:30:00-08:00
Subject: INTERNAL: Aegis Retail — quick decision notes (peering vs privatelink vs vpn)
Attachments: calc-burst-latency.xlsx (application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet)

Ben/Marcus — looping you in per our brief. Below are my quick notes after reviewing Sara's diagram and requirements. No customer-facing text here, just our internal tradeoffs and a recommended config to propose.

Context:
- Customer requires source-IP visibility for internal rate limits and log correlation.
- Baseline 120 req/s, bursts ~350 req/s; they want predictable SLOs and audited flows.
- Multi-AZ deployment on their side; they prefer to avoid long cross-account networking lead-times.

Options analysis:
1) VPC peering
  - Pros: L3 connectivity; source IP preserved end-to-end; simple packet flow; low per-packet AWS charges.
  - Cons: Cross-account peering increases route table complexity; route propagation risk across spokes; not ideal multi-region; harder to centrally enforce service-level routing policies; can't easily restrict service to a single app port without extra proxies.
  - Operational impact: We'll need peering acceptance, route table updates, and a strict runbook for RLS/RT control. Higher blast radius.

2) PrivateLink (interface endpoint)
  - Pros: Strong isolation (ENI-based), minimal route table changes on customer side, easy to expose a single service port, fits our private control plane model, better for compliance since access is explicit.
  - Cons: Depending on implementation, source-IP may appear as the endpoint ENI (we need to instrument X-Forwarded-For or preserve via UDP/TCP passthrough if possible); per-GB data charges and ENI costs apply; DNS & cert validation required.
  - Operational impact: Need to publish guides for customers on Private DNS names or split-horizon DNS, and ensure mTLS at the application layer when source-IP is required for auditability.

3) Site-to-site VPN (IPSec)
  - Pros: Familiar model for enterprise security teams, can be used as HA/burst path, supports IP visibility depending on NAT design, encrypts traffic across public internet.
  - Cons: Latency variance, tunnel management complexity, throughput limits without HA (BGP-based failover adds complexity), longer procurement lead time for firewalls and HA tunnels.
  - Operational impact: We'll need an NOC playbook, monitoring for tunnel flapping, and a way to shift traffic automatically during periods of congestion.

Recommendation (short):
- Primary: PrivateLink (interface endpoint) with explicit attestation in our onboarding docs. Implement token-level identity + mTLS so we do not rely solely on source-IP for auth/audit.
- Secondary/fallback: Site-to-site VPN (IPSec) as an optional overflow path; use it for day-1 bridge access and as a backup when PrivateLink capacity hits limits.
- Avoid: Full VPC peering unless the customer insists on L3 flattening and agrees to additional guardrails; reserve peering for cases where source-IP preservation is non-negotiable and both parties accept the operational burden.

Operational checklist highlights (for the proposal):
- DNS: Private hosted zone; conditional forwarders; document split-horizon behavior.
- Certs: Single-purpose certs for endpoint service; recommend mTLS termination at edge + app-level certs.
- NAT/Source IP: If PrivateLink, plan to add X-Forwarded-For and a lightweight proxy to capture origin; if peering, audit route tables and ensure no unexpected route propagation.
- Monitoring: token-level latency, per-route egress cost reporting, VPN tunnel health metrics.
- Capacity: Attach is a quick calc for burst sizing — if they want <100 ms P95 during bursts, we need to size private pool capacity for sustained 400 req/s headroom.

I'll draft the short decision memo for Sara and propose PrivateLink + VPN fallback. Ben: can you quickly sanity-check MTU/NAT notes? Marcus: can you add a short paragraph about deployment runbook (onboarding steps, required firewall rules, expected lead-times)?

Thanks,
Kim

Hi Sara — following up with our recommended approach and a short ops checklist (attached). Summary recommendation: PrivateLink (interface endpoint) as the primary connectivity pattern, with an optional site-to-site IPSec VPN for fallback/burst overflow.

Why PrivateLink first:
- Minimal route table changes in customer VPCs and small blast radius (good for audit/compliance).
- Easy to expose a single service port and control access via ENI security groups and resource policies.
- Fits Redwood Private control plane model and simplifies cross-account access governance.

Fallback VPN rationale:
- Use as a day-1 bridge for your ops team or as an overflow path during sustained bursts beyond the private pool capacity.
- We'll provide a runbook for HA tunnels (BGP where available) and a monitoring integration to detect failover.

Practical items for your team to prepare:
- Provide NOC contact and firewall/public IP ranges we should expect to terminate VPNs from.
- Confirm whether preserving exact source-IP in our app logs is a hard requirement; if so we should schedule a brief architecture call to discuss either peering (tradeoffs) or implementing an idempotent X-Forwarded-For path with PrivateLink + proxy.
- DNS: decide on private hosted zone vs split-horizon; our docs show both patterns and we'll walk through in the session.

Next step: does Thu 11/16 at 10:00 PT work for a 30-minute working session? I'll invite Ben and Marcus from our side to cover MTU/NAT concerns, runbook items, and capacity sizing.

Thanks — happy to iterate after the call.

Best regards,
Kimberly Park
